title: How a new shortcut makes everyone's drive longer
description:
4,000 drivers, two routes, each with a bridge that always takes 45 minutes and a town road that takes one minute per 100 cars. Traffic splits in half and everyone gets home in 65 minutes. Add a free shortcut between the two town roads and every driver takes it, because it's always the fastest choice: now both town roads carry 4,000 cars, the trip takes 80 minutes, and going back to a bridge alone would take 85. Every driver chose well and everyone lost 15 minutes. This is Braess's paradox (Dietrich Braess, 1968); Stuttgart's traffic only improved in 1969 after a newly built road was closed again.

Numbers checked in code (the equilibrium times and a 100,000-move simulation of drivers switching routes). Source: Wikipedia, Braess's paradox.

beats.say: Your drive: 65 minutes. Add a shortcut: 80.
No crash, and the shortcut takes zero minutes. Every driver just picks the fastest route.
4,000 drivers, two routes. Each has a bridge that always takes 45 minutes, and a town road: one minute for every 100 cars on it.
Traffic splits in half. 2,000 cars on each town road is 20 minutes, plus the bridge. 65.
Now open a free shortcut. Town road, shortcut, town road, and skip both bridges. The first driver gets home in 40.
So everyone copies them. That's the trap.
Now each town road has 4,000 cars. 40 plus 40 is 80. Go back to a bridge alone? 85. Nobody can switch back.
Every driver chose the fastest road, and everyone lost 15 minutes. In 1969, Stuttgart closed a brand new road, and its traffic got better.
